# Introduction

CITE-seq and similar assays measure proteins on single cells with
antibody-derived tags (ADTs). Not every ADT count in a droplet comes from
the cell's own proteins. DecontPro (Yin et al. 2024) splits each count into
three parts:

- **Native:** ADTs bound to the cell's own proteins. Cells of the same type
  share a native profile.
- **Ambient:** ADTs floating in the cell suspension that were captured
  along with the cell. One ambient profile is shared by the whole dataset.
- **Background:** other non-specific signal in the droplet.

DecontPro estimates the three parts with a Bayesian model fitted by Stan,
and returns the native part as the decontaminated counts.

# Installation

The decontX package, which contains DecontPro, can be installed from
Bioconductor:

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("decontX")
```

Then the package can be loaded in R using the following command:

```{r load, message=FALSE}
library(decontX)
```

To see the latest updates and releases or to post a bug, see our GitHub page
at https://github.com/campbio/decontX.

# Importing data

We use the cord blood CITE-seq data from the SingleCellMultiModal package.
Only the ADT counts and the cell annotations are downloaded (about 0.3 MB).

```{r import_data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(SingleCellMultiModal)

# Download the ADT counts and the cell annotations
cordBlood <- CITEseq(
  "cord_blood",
  modes = c("scADT_Counts", "coldata_scRNAseq"),
  dry.run = FALSE
)

# The ADT count matrix: one row per ADT, one column per droplet
allAdtCounts <- experiments(cordBlood)$scADT
dim(allAdtCounts)
```

The matrix holds 13 ADTs and 7,858 droplets. Every droplet is a called
cell, one that cell-calling software such as CellRanger judged to contain a
cell. DecontPro takes this filtered matrix, not the empty droplets.

# Cell types

DecontPro needs the cell type of each droplet. It learns one native profile
per cell type, so the labels should group cells whose proteins look alike.
The cord blood data come with cell-type labels:

```{r cell_types}
# The cell type of each droplet, in the order of the matrix columns
allCellTypes <- colData(cordBlood)[colnames(allAdtCounts), "celltype"]

# The number of droplets of each cell type
table(allCellTypes, useNA = "ifany")
```

DecontPro needs a label for every droplet. 158 droplets have none, so we
keep the 7,700 labelled ones:

```{r keep_labelled}
# Find the droplets that have a cell type
hasLabel <- !is.na(allCellTypes)

# Keep their counts and cell types
labelledCounts <- allAdtCounts[, hasLabel]
labelledCellTypes <- allCellTypes[hasLabel]
```

To keep this vignette fast, we sample 500 droplets. Don't subsample your
own data: DecontPro estimates the ambient profile from all the droplets it
is given, so a subsample, especially a biased one, can bias that estimate.

```{r subsample}
# Sample 500 droplets at random
set.seed(42)
sampledDroplets <- sample(ncol(labelledCounts), 500)

# The counts and cell types of the sampled droplets
adtCounts <- labelledCounts[, sampledDroplets]
cellTypes <- labelledCellTypes[sampledDroplets]

# The number of sampled droplets of each cell type
table(cellTypes)
```

The labels can be character strings, as here, integers or a factor. With
your own data, cluster labels work too: for example, Seurat's cluster
identities can be passed as they are, with `Idents(seuratObject)`. Very fine
clusters split a cell type into small groups, each with its own native
profile; broader cell types are often more useful.

# Running DecontPro

DecontPro takes the count matrix and the cell types:

```{r decontPro}
# Decontaminate the counts, without printing Stan's progress
decontResult <- decontPro(adtCounts, cellTypes, verbose = FALSE)
```

`verbose = FALSE` hides DecontPro's messages and Stan's progress, which is
long. If the fit fails, Stan's output is shown anyway.

# The output

The result is a list:

```{r output_names}
# The elements of the result
names(decontResult)
```

- `parameters`: the model's estimates, described below.
- `decontaminated_counts`: the native part, the counts that come from the
  cell's own proteins.
- `ambient_counts`: the ambient part.
- `background_counts`: the background part.

The three count matrices have one row per ADT and one column per droplet,
with the row and column names of the input. Each count is split into the
three parts, so they add up to the original counts:

```{r output_check}
# Add the three parts together
summedParts <- decontResult$decontaminated_counts +
  decontResult$ambient_counts +
  decontResult$background_counts

# Compare the sum with the original counts
all.equal(summedParts, adtCounts)
```

The share of all counts that DecontPro called ambient or background:

```{r output_share}
# Share of all counts called ambient
sum(decontResult$ambient_counts) / sum(adtCounts)

# Share of all counts called background
sum(decontResult$background_counts) / sum(adtCounts)
```

`decontResult$parameters` holds:

- `delta_sd`, `background_sd`: the values of the two priors used in the
  fit.
- `r_est`: the native profile of each cell type, with one row per cell
  type, named by its label, and one column per ADT. Each row sums to 1.
- `p_est`: the ambient profile, the share of each ADT among ambient counts.
  It sums to 1.
- `delta_est`: for each ADT (row) in each droplet (column), the weight of
  the ambient profile in the part of the counts that isn't background; the
  native profile gets the rest (1 minus this weight).
- `delta_mean_est`: for each droplet, the mean level of `delta_est`.
- `background_est`: for each ADT (row) in each droplet (column), the
  background as a proportion of the droplet's total count.
- `background_mean_est`: for each ADT, the mean level of `background_est`.

Apart from `p_est` and the rows of `r_est`, these estimates don't carry
names yet. Their ADTs follow the rows of the counts, and their droplets the
columns.

# Tuning the priors

The density of each ADT before and after decontamination shows whether the
results are reasonable. Many ADTs have two peaks: a low one from cells that
don't express the protein, whose counts are mostly contamination, and a
high one from cells that do. Decontamination should move the low peak
toward zero and leave the high peak in place.

```{r density_default, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
# Density of six ADTs before and after decontamination
plotDensity(
  adtCounts,
  decontResult$decontaminated_counts,
  c("CD3", "CD4", "CD8", "CD14", "CD16", "CD19")
)
```

With the default priors, little is removed here: most of the low CD8 peak
stays where it was, and only part of the low CD3 and CD4 peaks moves toward
zero.

A prior is the model's assumption about a value before it sees the data.
Two priors, each a standard deviation, control how much DecontPro removes:

- `deltaSd` (default 2e-5): how much the ambient level can vary from one
  ADT to another within a droplet.
- `backgroundSd` (default 2e-6): how much the background level of an ADT
  can vary from one droplet to another.

Larger values let DecontPro assign more of each count to contamination;
smaller values remove less. We tested the defaults on datasets of 5,000 to
10,000 droplets and 10 to 30 ADTs, and the results were reasonable. A
smaller or a more contaminated dataset may need larger priors. Our 500
droplets are a small dataset, so we try priors 3 times the defaults:

```{r decontPro_tuned}
# Decontaminate again with priors 3 times the defaults
tunedResult <- decontPro(
  adtCounts,
  cellTypes,
  deltaSd = 6e-5,
  backgroundSd = 6e-6,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r density_tuned, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
# Density of the same ADTs after the second fit
plotDensity(
  adtCounts,
  tunedResult$decontaminated_counts,
  c("CD3", "CD4", "CD8", "CD14", "CD16", "CD19")
)
```

Now more of the low peaks of CD3, CD4 and CD8 moves toward zero, while the
high peaks stay. These results are close to what the default priors give on
all 7,700 labelled droplets. We fitted those once, outside this vignette:
for these 500 droplets, the counts decontaminated here and those from the
fit on all droplets have a correlation of 0.99 on a log scale.

CD4 is a useful check: it has three peaks, and the middle one comes from
monocytes, which express some CD4. Only the lowest peak should move toward
zero. The middle peak gets a little lower here but stays in place. Priors
that are too large remove real signal: at 10 times the defaults, the middle
CD4 peak is pushed down toward zero, and the high CD14 peak of the
monocytes shrinks.

The decontaminated counts can also be compared within each cell type:

```{r box_by_cell_type, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
# Counts of four ADTs in each cell type, before and after decontamination
plotBoxByCluster(
  adtCounts,
  tunedResult$decontaminated_counts,
  cellTypes,
  c("CD3", "CD4", "CD8", "CD16")
)
```

Each protein should stay high in the cell types that express it and fall in
the others. Here CD3 stays high in the T cells and falls close to zero in B
cells and natural killer cells; CD8 stays high in CD8 T cells and natural
killer cells and falls in B cells and CD4 T cells.

Cell types with only a few droplets in this sample, such as T-cells (2
droplets) and Precursors (8), are estimated poorly: their native profiles
rest on very few droplets, and their results differ the most from the fit
on all droplets. This is another
reason to run DecontPro on all of your droplets.

# With empty droplets {#background}

By default, DecontPro estimates the ambient profile from the filtered
matrix. If you have the raw matrix, which holds every droplet barcode, you
can estimate it from the empty droplets instead, with the `background`
argument. Only the total of each ADT across those droplets is used, so
`background` sets the ambient profile and nothing else.

The cord blood data don't include the raw matrix, so this code is a
template. For data processed with CellRanger, the raw matrix is in the
`"outs/raw_feature_bc_matrix/"` subfolder of each sample directory, and
singleCellTK imports it when the `dataType` argument is set to "raw".
Replace the path with your own sample directory and `cellTypes` with your
own labels:

```{r background_template, eval=FALSE}
library(singleCellTK)

# Import the filtered matrix (the called cells) and the raw matrix.
# Use the same sample directory for both, so the barcodes match.
sceFiltered <- importCellRanger(
  sampleDirs = "path/to/sample1/",
  dataType = "filtered"
)
sceRaw <- importCellRanger(
  sampleDirs = "path/to/sample1/",
  dataType = "raw"
)

# Keep the ADT rows of each matrix
isAdtFiltered <- rowData(sceFiltered)$feature_type == "Antibody Capture"
adtFiltered <- counts(sceFiltered)[isAdtFiltered, ]
isAdtRaw <- rowData(sceRaw)$feature_type == "Antibody Capture"
adtRaw <- counts(sceRaw)[isAdtRaw, ]

# Keep the empty droplets: remove the barcodes of the called cells
isEmpty <- !colnames(adtRaw) %in% colnames(adtFiltered)
adtEmpty <- adtRaw[, isEmpty]

# Estimate the ambient profile from the empty droplets
emptyDropletResult <- decontPro(
  adtFiltered,
  cellTypes,
  background = adtEmpty
)
```

Unlike `decontX()`, DecontPro doesn't remove the called cells from
`background` itself, so remove them first, as above. When both matrices
have row names, the ADTs are matched by name: ADTs in `background` that
aren't in the counts are dropped, and every ADT of the counts must be in
`background`. Without row names, the rows must be in the same order.

# Runtime and reproducibility

The run time grows with the number of ADTs times the number of droplets.
Each fit in this vignette, 13 ADTs in 500 droplets, takes one to two minutes
on a laptop; all 7,700 labelled droplets take about 25 minutes per fit.
Stan writes a temporary file during the fit, which DecontPro deletes when
the fit ends.

Stan's fit is random. DecontPro sets Stan's seed with the `seed` argument
(default 12345), so the same counts, cell types, priors and seed give the
same results. `iter` (default 50000) is the maximum number of iterations;
the fit usually stops earlier, when it converges.

# Frequently asked questions

## Can I give DecontPro the raw matrix with every droplet?

No. DecontPro models each droplet as a cell of a given type, so the counts
must be the filtered matrix, with the called cells only. The empty droplets
can still help, through the `background` argument (see
[With empty droplets](#background)).
